content: Streptomycin is prescribed for the treatment of moderate to severe infections caused by microorganisms that are susceptible to its antibacterial effects. Its use is specifically indicated in the following conditions: Mycobacterium tuberculosis Streptomycin is recommended as part of the initial treatment regimen for tuberculosis (TB) in combination with isoniazid (INH), rifampin, and pyrazinamide. This recommendation comes from the Advisory Council for the Elimination of Tuberculosis, the American Thoracic Society, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Streptomycin or ethambutol is added as a fourth drug unless the likelihood of resistance to INH or rifampin is very low. Once susceptibility testing results are available, the necessity of the fourth drug should be reassessed. Historically, when the national rate of primary resistance to INH was less than 4% and either stable or declining, twoor three-drug regimens were considered sufficient. If current community rates of INH resistance remain below 4%, a regimen with fewer than four drugs may be appropriate. Streptomycin is also indicated for TB treatment in cases where one or more of the primary drugs (INH, rifampin, or pyrazinamide) cannot be used due to toxicity or intolerance. The management of tuberculosis has become increasingly complex due to rising rates of drug resistance and the co-occurrence of HIV infection. In such cases, consultation with experts in TB treatment is advisable. Non-tuberculosis Infections Streptomycin is reserved for treating infections caused by bacteria that are proven to be susceptible to its effects and for which alternative, less toxic treatments are not suitable. These infections include: Plague caused by Pasteurella pestis. Tularemia caused by Francisella tularensis. Brucellosis caused by Brucella species. Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) caused by Calymmatobacterium granulomatis. Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Haemophilus influenzae infections (respiratory, endocardial, and meningeal), used in combination with another antibacterial agent. Klebsiella pneumoniae pneumonia, used in combination with another antibacterial agent. Urinary tract infections caused by Escherichia coli, Proteus species, Aerobacter aerogenes, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterococcus faecalis. Endocardial infections caused by Streptococcus viridans and Enterococcus faecalis, used in combination with penicillin. Gram-negative bacillary bacteremia, used in combination with another antibacterial agent. To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria and preserve the efficacy of streptomycin and other antibiotics, streptomycin should only be used to treat or prevent infections that are confirmed or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility data are available, they should guide the selection or adjustment of therapy. In the absence of such data, local epidemiological trends and susceptibility patterns should inform the choice of empiric treatment.
